# Intro

## Outline

1) Distinguish between atomic commits and bulk dumps.

2) Structure a professional `README.md` that enables one-line project execution.

3) Reviewing `environment.yml` files.


## Main Idea

\

::: {.poll}
If a collaborator (or grader) clones your repository today, can they reproduce your entire analysis?
:::


# Git History

## Examples {.smaller}

👎 

```{.markdown filename="Poor Commits" code-line-numbers="false"}
Merge classroom repository
Add Serena Williams plot reproduction
Initial Commit
```

. . .

\

👍

```{.markdown filename="Good Commits" code-line-numbers="false"}
Document project purpose, setup, data definitions, and report workflow
Ignore Python caches and local system files
Add standalone HTML report with embedded career plot
Add the supplied PDF report
Add report narrative matching the supplied PDF
Add reproduced Serena Williams career scatterplot
Add cleaned Serena match data with ages and outcomes
Preserve Tennis Abstract raw career data snapshot
Add Make targets to build and clean data, plot, and reports
Define Conda environment for data processing and report generation
... # etc
```


## The Bulk "Submit Button" Commit

- [No Rollback Capability:]{.bold-hilit} If an analysis script breaks at hour 10, 
a bulk commit forces you to discard everything rather than rewinding to a functional state.

- [Opaque Collaboration:]{.bold-hilit} In group settings, bulk commits create 
massive merge conflicts and hide individual provenance.

- [Data Dumping:]{.bold-hilit} Bulk commits often accidentally check in binary outputs, 
credentials, or multi-gigabyte raw files.


## Atomic Commits

An atomic commit encapsulates one logical unit of work e.g., 

+ `"adding a data preprocessing function"`
+ `"fixing a plotting script bug"`
+ `"updating the environment.yml"`


## Advantages of Atomic Commits

If you commit:

::: {.nonincremental}
- a bug fix,
- an environment change, 
- and a data-cleaning script 
:::

in three separate commits, you can easily revert just the broken 
data-cleaning script (`git revert <commit-hash>`) while keeping your bug fix intact.


## Bulk Commits (Don't ❗️)

\

While taking a "snapshot" of several (e.g. 10) modified files at the end of a long work 
session feels convenient, it breaks the core benefits of version control. 

. . .

Why?

If all 10 changes live in a single massive commit, reverting the bug means 
throwing away hours of unrelated, functional work---or manually sifting through 
hundreds of lines of code to fix it by hand.


## Bulk Commits (Don't ❗️)

\

With bulk commits a reviewer cannot meaningfully audit a single pull request or commit that reads:

```
+12,450 lines / -3,200 lines across 40 files.
```

. . .

\

Smaller, logical commits tell a readable story. A reviewer can follow your 
thought process step-by-step rather than drowning in a massive wall of code differences
(`git diff`)


## Bulk Commits (Don't ❗️)

When working on collaborative projects or multi-branch workflows:

Smaller, frequent commits touch fewer lines of code at a time, 
making automatic merges smooth.

When you finally push a bulk commit, it frequently conflicts with your collaborators' work, 
creating complex merge conflicts that require hours of manual reconstruction.


## Risk of Accidental File Leaks & Repository Bloat

When developers run `git add .` and commit everything in bulk without inspecting 
their staging area, they frequently check in files that should never enter version control:

- Large Datasets / Binaries: Large CSVs, SQLite databases, or model weights that 
permanently bloat the `.git` folder history.

- System junk: `.DS_Store files`, build artifacts, or temporary editor files.

- Sensitive Information: API keys, passwords, or local file system path configurations.


## Rule of Thumb

\

As a rule of thumb, [one commit should represent one logical unit of work.]{.bold-hilit}

\

[A Good Test:]{.mdlit} If your commit message needs the word ["AND"]{.hilit} 
to describe what you did (e.g., 
`"Cleaned data matrix AND added plotting script AND updated environment specs"`), 
it should be split into three separate commits.


# README Architecture

## The "README as an API" Principle

\

A `README.md` is not just a summary cover sheet; it is the instruction manual 
for your computational pipeline.


## 5+1 mandatory sections in README

- Title
- Overview (about)
- Repository structure (file structure)
- Environment setup 
- Reproduction instructions
- License*


## Filestructure in README

Benefits:

1) Establishes Instant Spatial Orientation (Mental Model)

2) Clarifies Data Provenance & File Roles

3) Discovers Relative Paths & Eliminates Path Confusion

4) Serves as Self-Documenting Infrastructure

5) Exposes Messy Repository Hygiene (The "Messy Room" Test)


## Establishes Instant Spatial Orientation (Mental Model)

When a collaborator, reviewer, or grader clones your repository, they are 
looking at a blank slate.

- Without a tree, they have to manually click through nested subfolders to 
figure out where scripts, datasets, and configurations reside.

- A directory tree provides a 3-second visual map of the entire codebase. 
It immediately communicates the project’s layout without requiring the reader 
to explore the file system manually.


## Clarifies Data Provenance & File Roles

Filename extensions (like `.csv`, `.py`, `.ipynb`, or `.rds`) don't tell the full 
story of why a file exists or how it should be treated.

- [Separating Raw vs. Processed Data:]{.bold-hilit} A directory tree visually enforces the 
golden rule of reproducible research: raw data must be immutable. 
Annotating `data/raw/` in your tree explicitly warns users never to overwrite original files.

- [Distinguishing Source Code from Notebooks:]{.bold-hilit} It clarifies which files 
are modular, reusable scripts (e.g., `scripts/clean_data.py`) versus interactive 
exploratory narratives (e.g., `notebooks/exploratory.ipynb`).


## Closing Thoughts

- Writing clean code is only half the battle in modern data science. 

\

- If your work cannot be re-built automatically by an independent researcher 
using your version-control record and environment specs, the results are incomplete. 

\

- Treat your repository as a publication in itself.
